title: Attached Possessive Pronouns — Plural Forms (نَا / كُمْ / هُمْ)

steps.title: The same suffixes, for a group
body: You already know ـِي (my), ـكَ (your, m.), ـكِ (your, f.), ـهُ (his), and ـهَا (her) attach directly to a noun to show possession. Three more suffixes do the exact same job for a group: ـنَا (our), ـكُمْ (your, plural), and ـهُمْ (their).

بَيْتُنَا ("our house") attaches ـنَا — no gender split, the same for any group that includes "me." أَيْنَ كِتَابُكُمْ؟ ("where is your book?") attaches ـكُمْ when speaking to more than one person. مَدْرَسَتُهُمْ ("their school") attaches ـهُمْ.

ـكُمْ and ـهُمْ are the masculine/mixed-group forms — the same default you already saw on the independent pronoun هُمْ ("they, masculine/mixed group"). Arabic also has separate forms for an all-female group (ـكُنَّ, ـهُنَّ) and for exactly two people (ـكُمَا, ـهُمَا) — rare enough at this level to name and leave for later, the same way dual relative pronouns did.

steps.title: Three plural suffixes
steps.intro: Read each sentence and find the possessive suffix, then check whose it is. Tap 🔊 to hear any line.

steps.title: Whose house?
steps.explanation: ـنَا is "our" — no gender split, attaching the same way for any group that includes the speaker.

steps.title: Speaking to more than one person
steps.prompt: How many people is this question addressed to?

options.label: More than one — ـكُمْ is the plural "your"

steps.explanation: ـكَ (singular, masculine) and ـكُمْ (plural) are different suffixes — كِتَابُكَ would ask one man, كِتَابُكُمْ asks a group.

steps.title: A group's school
steps.prompt: Why does this word end in ـهُمْ here, instead of ـهُ?

options.label: The school belongs to a group of people, not one person
ـهُمْ and ـهُ mean exactly the same thing
مَدْرَسَة requires a special suffix no other noun uses

steps.explanation: ـهُ is "his" (one person); ـهُمْ is "their" (a group) — the same suffix mechanic, just scaled up from one antecedent to many.

steps.title: The possessive paradigm, completed
steps.message: ـِي، ـكَ، ـكِ، ـهُ، ـهَا for one person; ـنَا، ـكُمْ، ـهُمْ for a group — eight suffixes covering the everyday cases. The all-female-group and dual forms are still ahead.
